DOI: [10.7554/eLife.04241.025](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.04241.025)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for sending your work entitled “Decoding a neural circuit controlling global animal state in C. elegans” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Catherine Dulac (Senior editor), Graeme Davis (Reviewing editor), and 2 reviewers (Scott Emmons and L René García), both of whom are expert in the research area of the manuscript.

The Reviewing editor and the reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

Laurent et al. are reverse engineering circuit function in C. elegans. The circuit they are studying is one that results in multiple behavioral and physiological changes in response to elevated oxygen levels. Laurent et al. use the full range of experimental tools available in C. elegans, including cell ablation, Ca2+ imaging, optogenetic stimulation, cell-specific expression of transgenes to block chemical transmission and neuropeptide transmission or the cell-specific rescue of such functions in mutants, and automated behavioral analysis. They show that they can identify several layers of neurons in the pathway. Overall the data are convincing and clearly presented in the figures.

Both reviewers consider the topic interesting and consider the data well presented and supportive of your major conclusions. As you will see from the comments, both reviewers recommend significant re-writing of the text to make the manuscript accessible to the general audience of eLife. Both reviewers list a series of suggestions that you can use as a guide to improve accessibility of your text.

Reviewer #1:

1) The authors should choose one way to refer to npr-1 “mutants.” This can be very confusing because the N2 allele is itself a “mutant.” The authors refer to the null allele in various places as npr-1, npr-1 mutant, npr-1 loss of function, npr-1(null), npr-1(ad609), and npr-1(ky13). As ky13 is specifically referred to as a null, what is ad609? In the second sentence of the Results they already refer to “npr-1 mutants.” They should explain that by this they mean a null mutation (is that right?). They should specify how they intend to refer to the null allele, and then stick to that one form throughout the paper (except where they want to specifically indicate ad609 vs ky13).

2) The first section of results on changes in gene expression is very confusing and needs rewriting for clarity. URX, AQR, and PQR neurons control “part, but not all, of this response.” What part? Where is the clear statement of the number of genes that change their expression between 7% and 21% O2 in gcy-36(+) but not gcy-36(–)? Figure 1 does not show this and therefore does not show what it says it does in its heading. It shows genes that change between gcy-36(+) vs gcy-36(–) at a single O2 concentration (21%).

3) Start the third section of Results by saying: “Among the three O2 sensing neurons, the URX neurons uniquely make gap junctions and reciprocal synaptic connections with the RMG interneurons.” Since in the forgoing URX has always been mentioned as one of a group of three sensory neurons, along with AQR and PQR, the reader makes a wrong assumption and puzzles, why doesn't RMG respond to AQR and PQR when URX is ablated?

4) For all their references to neural connectivity in the C. elegans wiring diagram, the authors should not only refer to the canonical White et al., paper but also to the data on the WormWiring.org website. The Emmons laboratory has reevaluated the original electron micrographs and has found some discrepancies.

5) The authors show that stimulating RMG can induce the high O2 behavioral response, so its activity is sufficient. But is it necessary? Where is the RMG ablation result? Has this been published already? Yes, I see, it is in Busch et al., Nature Neuroscience, 2012. This should be referred to, as well as their earlier data that the other two O2 sensing neurons signal via peptides to a different target. It would be helpful to make clear that the present paper focuses exclusively on the URX-RMG pathway.

Reviewer #2:

1) The meat of the study begins with Figure 2. As a reader that is not intimately acquainted with the O2-sensing circuitry, I found it helpful to draw out the circuitry and include where ocr-2, npr-1, tax-2, flip-11, etc. were expressed. As I was going through each of the experiments, I referred to my drawing to get my bearings on which part of the circuitry the authors were probing. I suggest that the authors provide a similar circuit roadmap as supplementary figure, to provide a reference for the reader to follow throughout the paper.

2) Beginning in Figure 2, as well as in the other figures, I was not sure what N refers to. For example in Figure 2B, I did not know if N referred to the number of animals? Or Did N refer to number of times that a 7%-21%-7% train was conducted on a limited number of animals, (if so how many animals?). This could be elaborated in the figure legend. Also in Figure 3A, 3B, 3C, 3D, and elsewhere, what does N> (some number) mean? The graphs have SEMs, so there must be a discreet sample size.

3) In Figure D, E and F, (as well as in later experiments), the animals are not reported to contain the lite-1 mutation, but in Figure 2J and 2K, the strains did contain lite-1; is this just a typo? On the scopes in my lab, the 430 to 480 nM light will elicit an escape response in the worm (unless they are lite-1), if the light is too intense. You might want to mention in your Material and methods how you were able get around this. I noticed in Figure 5I and 5J (no retinal) that the light source on your set-up did not irritate the animals, so you might want to mention that early on.

4) You should clarify in the Material and methods what criteria you chose to pick the intervals (black bars and red bars) that you did your statistics.

5) In the subsection headed “ASK, ASH and ADL sensory neuron which have gap junctions with RMG are not required for the O2-evoked switch in behavioral state”, I was not sure whether the punchline was that these 3 neurons were not relevant for O2 sensation, or that these 3 neurons were redundant with each other for O2-responses. The latter seemed to be the case given the following section on ocr-2 mutant phenotype, but stronger wording should clarify things.

6) In the subsection headed “Homeostatic re-setting of downstream O2 responsive circuits according to input”, the first sentence, “… alters circuitry by a homeostatic mechanism, such as…”: the use of the word homeostatic was not clear to me. My imagination (after pondering this for minutes upon minutes) started to come up with wild ideas of acclimation and desensitization after prolonged stimulation, with the ultimate equilibration to a default behavioral state. Then my imagination wanted to know what is that default behavioral state, and this distracting thinking is not what your paper is about. If I interpret your paper's point correctly, it is about how the regulation of immediate locomotor transitions are realized in a physical set of cell connections. So again, maybe more elaboration and keeping the reader's train-of-thought from digressing can help this section.

7) In the subsection “TRPV channel activity alters O2 circuit function upstream of NPR-1”, the last sentence of the first paragraph (“Instead, we suggest that TRPV dependent currents in ASH…”) needs more elaboration; there is more than one concept being stated in this sentence. This sentence puzzled me, and I am guessing (and probably wrongly), that the authors are suggesting that the ASH and ADL have the potential to leach away some excitatory factor from RMG via gap junctions; however, OCR-2 in ASH and ADL can attenuate this? Anyway clarification should make their concepts more obvious. Similarly, three sentences later, the statement, “as the tetanus toxin experiments suggested…”, also contained multiple concepts. This sentence also took me awhile to digest. Again more clarification should make this section easier to understand, and help put the next section in more context.

claims.claim: For 71 out of 72 genes, disrupting gcy-35 had a similar effect on gene expression as growing npr-1 animals at 7% O2.
claims.source: For almost all of these genes, 71/72, disrupting gcy-35 had a similar effect on gene expression as growing npr-1 animals at 7% O2 (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RNA sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: Genes whose expression was regulated by O2 experience in a GCY-35-dependent way encoded proteins involved in metabolism.
claims.source: Genes whose expression was regulated by O2 experience in a GCY-35-dependent way encoded proteins involved in metabolism (e.g., elo-6, a polyunsaturated fatty acid elongase; folt-2, a folate transporter; mai-2, a mitochondrial intrinsic ATPase inhibitor protein), oxidation–reduction reactions (e.g., the cytochrome p450s, cyp-35C1 and cyp-34A2), and proteolysis (e.g., the cathepsins cpr-4 and cpr-6), suggesting broad changes not limited to the nervous system (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RNA sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: Genes whose expression was regulated by O2 experience in a GCY-35-dependent way encoded proteins involved in oxidation-reduction reactions.
claims.source: Genes whose expression was regulated by O2 experience in a GCY-35-dependent way encoded proteins involved in metabolism (e.g., elo-6, a polyunsaturated fatty acid elongase; folt-2, a folate transporter; mai-2, a mitochondrial intrinsic ATPase inhibitor protein), oxidation–reduction reactions (e.g., the cytochrome p450s, cyp-35C1 and cyp-34A2), and proteolysis (e.g., the cathepsins cpr-4 and cpr-6), suggesting broad changes not limited to the nervous system (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RNA sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: Genes whose expression was regulated by O2 experience in a GCY-35-dependent way encoded proteins involved in proteolysis.
claims.source: Genes whose expression was regulated by O2 experience in a GCY-35-dependent way encoded proteins involved in metabolism (e.g., elo-6, a polyunsaturated fatty acid elongase; folt-2, a folate transporter; mai-2, a mitochondrial intrinsic ATPase inhibitor protein), oxidation–reduction reactions (e.g., the cytochrome p450s, cyp-35C1 and cyp-34A2), and proteolysis (e.g., the cathepsins cpr-4 and cpr-6), suggesting broad changes not limited to the nervous system (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RNA sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: npr-1 animals increased their speed of movement when exposed to 21% O2 in the presence of food.
claims.source: When exposed to 21% O2 in the presence of food, npr-1 animals not only increased their speed of movement (Busch et al., 2012) (Figure 1A), but also increased the persistence of their forward travel by inhibiting spontaneous short reversals (Figure 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Busch et al., 2012 and by Figure 1A.

claims.claim: npr-1 animals increased the persistence of their forward travel by inhibiting spontaneous short reversals when exposed to 21% O2 in the presence of food.
claims.source: When exposed to 21% O2 in the presence of food, npr-1 animals not only increased their speed of movement (Busch et al., 2012) (Figure 1A), but also increased the persistence of their forward travel by inhibiting spontaneous short reversals (Figure 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claims.claim: Mutations in gcy-35 disrupted O2 modulation of both speed and spontaneous reversal frequency in npr-1 animals.
claims.source: Mutations in gcy-35, which abolish the O2 responsiveness of URX, AQR, and PQR neurons, disrupted O2 modulation of both speed (Busch et al., 2012) and spontaneous reversal frequency (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Busch et al., 2012 and by Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Expressing gcy-35 selectively in URX neurons restored rapid movement and sustained inhibition of reversals at 21% O2 to gcy-35; npr-1 animals.
claims.source: Expressing gcy-35 selectively in URX neurons restored rapid movement and sustained inhibition of reversals at 21% O2.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: URX and RMG are connected by gap junctions and reciprocal synaptic connections.
claims.source: Among the three O2-sensing neurons, URX neurons uniquely make gap junctions and reciprocal synaptic connections with the RMG interneurons (White et al., 1986; wormwiring.org; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 1986 and wormwiring.org, and by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: RMG interneurons respond to a 7-21% rise in O2 with a sustained increase in Ca2+.
claims.source: The RMG interneurons respond to a 7–21% rise in O2 with a sustained increase in Ca2+, and ablating RMG disrupts behavioral responses evoked by this O2 switch (Busch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Busch et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Ablating RMG disrupts behavioral responses evoked by a 7-21% O2 switch.
claims.source: The RMG interneurons respond to a 7–21% rise in O2 with a sustained increase in Ca2+, and ablating RMG disrupts behavioral responses evoked by this O2 switch (Busch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Busch et al., 2012.

claims.claim: When URX was ablated, O2 stimuli failed to evoke Ca2+ responses in RMG.
claims.source: When URX was ablated, O2 stimuli failed to evoke Ca2+ responses in RMG (Figure 1D), and RMG Ca2+ resembled that found in tax-4 mutants, which lack the cGMP-gated channel required for URX, AQR, and PQR neurons to transduce O2 stimuli (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: RMG Ca2+ in URX-ablated animals resembled that found in tax-4 mutants.
claims.source: When URX was ablated, O2 stimuli failed to evoke Ca2+ responses in RMG (Figure 1D), and RMG Ca2+ resembled that found in tax-4 mutants, which lack the cGMP-gated channel required for URX, AQR, and PQR neurons to transduce O2 stimuli (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Stimulating RMG using channelrhodopsin-2 inhibited spontaneous reversals in npr-1 animals kept at 7% O2.
claims.source: Stimulating RMG inhibited spontaneous reversals and induced rapid and persistent forward movement for as long as blue light was on (Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: Stimulating RMG using channelrhodopsin-2 induced rapid and persistent forward movement in npr-1 animals kept at 7% O2.
claims.source: Stimulating RMG inhibited spontaneous reversals and induced rapid and persistent forward movement for as long as blue light was on (Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: URX neurons respond in a graded manner to changes in O2 between 7% and 21% in npr-1 animals.
claims.source: In npr-1 animals, URX neurons respond in a graded manner to changes in O2 between 7% and 21%, and evoke graded increases in locomotory rate according to final O2 concentration (Cheung et al., 2005; Busch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheung et al., 2005 and Busch et al., 2012.

claims.claim: URX neurons evoke graded increases in locomotory rate according to final O2 concentration in npr-1 animals.
claims.source: In npr-1 animals, URX neurons respond in a graded manner to changes in O2 between 7% and 21%, and evoke graded increases in locomotory rate according to final O2 concentration (Cheung et al., 2005; Busch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheung et al., 2005 and Busch et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The effects of activating RMG using ChR2 summated with input from the O2 sensory circuit.
claims.source: The effects of activating RMG using ChR2 summated with input from the O2 sensory circuit: animals kept at 21% reached higher speeds and inhibited reversals more strongly than animals kept at 7% (Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: Ablated animals (URX, AQR, PQR) robustly increased their speed and suppressed reversals upon light-activation of RMG.
claims.source: Ablated animals robustly increased their speed and suppressed reversals upon light-activation of RMG, both at 7% and at 21% O2 (Figure 1G,H).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claims.claim: The speed responses of URX, AQR, PQR ablated animals were not influenced by O2 levels.
claims.source: As expected if O2 input was lost, the speed responses of the ablated animals were not influenced by the O2 levels (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: npr-1 animals lacking RMG showed a much smaller URX Ca2+ response to a 7-21% O2 stimulus compared to mock ablated controls.
claims.source: npr-1 animals lacking RMG showed a much smaller URX Ca2+ response to a 7–21% O2 stimulus compared to mock ablated controls (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: Partial loss-of-function mutants of unc-64 syntaxin showed reduced Ca2+ levels in URX and RMG both at 7% and 21% O2.
claims.source: However, consistent with a role for synaptic input in sustaining URX excitability, partial loss-of-function mutants of unc-64 syntaxin, which have deficits in synaptic release, showed reduced Ca2+ levels in URX and RMG both at 7% and 21% O2 (Figure 1D,K).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and 1K.

claims.claim: URX neurons could still evoke Ca2+ responses in RMG in unc-64 mutants.
claims.source: URX neurons could still evoke Ca2+ responses in RMG in unc-64 mutants (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Expressing NPR-1 215V selectively in RMG reduces the locomotory activity of npr-1 animals.
claims.source: The RMG neurons are one site of action for this receptor: expressing NPR-1 215V selectively in RMG reduces the locomotory activity of npr-1 animals (Macosko et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Macosko et al., 2009.

claims.claim: npr-1 animals that expressed NPR-1 215V in RMG did not exhibit long-lasting changes in locomotion in response to changes in O2.
claims.source: npr-1 animals that expressed NPR-1 215V in RMG did not exhibit long-lasting changes in locomotion in response to changes in O2 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: npr-1 animals that expressed NPR-1 215V in RMG retained the transient bout of reversals and reorientation triggered by a sharp rise in O2.
claims.source: However, they retained the transient bout of reversals and reorientation triggered by a sharp rise in O2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: NPR-1 215V receptor signaling in RMG selectively suppresses the sustained switch in locomotory behavior evoked by high and low O2.
claims.source: Thus, NPR-1 215V receptor signaling in RMG selectively suppresses the sustained switch in locomotory behavior evoked by high and low O2.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claims.claim: FLP-21 peptide is an in vivo ligand for NPR-1.
claims.source: The FMRFamide neuropeptide encoded by the flp-21 gene is an in vivo ligand for NPR-1 (Rogers et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rogers et al., 2003.

claims.claim: flp-21 is expressed in several neurons, including RMG.
claims.source: flp-21 is expressed in several neurons, including RMG itself (Kim and Li, 2004; Macosko et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Li, 2004 and Macosko et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Deleting flp-21 caused animals expressing the natural npr-1 215F or derived npr-1 215V allele to increase the amplitude of their O2-evoked behavioral switch.
claims.source: Consistent with this, deleting flp-21 caused animals expressing the natural npr-1 215F or derived npr-1 215V allele, but not npr-1(null) mutants, to increase the amplitude of their O2-evoked behavioral switch (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-C.

claims.claim: N2 animals exhibited reduced Ca2+ responses in RMG compared to npr-1 mutants.
claims.source: N2 animals exhibited reduced Ca2+ responses in RMG compared to npr-1 mutants (Figure 2D), which would be consistent with NPR-1 215V inhibiting RMG Ca2+ signaling.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The promoter combination targeting YC2.60 expression to RMG drove lower expression in N2 compared to npr-1 animals.
claims.source: More importantly, the promoter combination targeting YC2.60 expression to RMG (pncs-1::cre and pflp-21::LoxP-STOP-LoxP::YC2.60) drove lower expression in N2 compared to npr-1 animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Lower sensor expression correlated with lower YFP/CFP ratio at 21% O2.
claims.source: Lower sensor expression correlated with lower YFP/CFP ratio at 21% O2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that sensor expression differences could account for much of the YFP/CFP ratio differences between N2 and npr-1 animals (see below for an explanation of why pflp-21 drove lower RMG expression in N2 compared to npr-1 animals).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Light activation of RMG triggered only a small increase in N2 locomotory activity, regardless of whether animals were kept at 21% or 7% O2.
claims.source: Consistent with this, light activation of RMG triggered only a small increase in N2 locomotory activity, regardless of whether animals were kept at 21% or 7% O2, and in marked contrast to its effects in npr-1 mutants (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: npr-1 mutants kept at 7% O2 had much lower Ca2+ in RMG compared to N2 animals kept at 21% O2, yet they responded to RMG ChR2 activation significantly more strongly.
claims.source: Most compellingly, although npr-1 mutants kept at 7% O2 had much lower Ca2+ in RMG compared to N2 animals kept at 21% O2 (Figure 2D), they responded to RMG ChR2 activation significantly more strongly (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: The NPR-1 215V and NPR-1 215F receptors can each couple to Go/i signaling following stimulation by FLP-21.
claims.source: In vitro work suggests that the NPR-1 215V and NPR-1 215F receptors can each couple to Go/i signaling following stimulation by FLP-21 (Rogers et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rogers et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The RGS protein EAT-16 terminates Gq signaling by activating intrinsic Gq GTPase activity.
claims.source: The RGS (regulator of G protein signaling) protein EAT-16 terminates Gq signaling by activating intrinsic Gq GTPase activity (Hajdu-Cronin et al., 1999); RSBP-1 (R7 binding protein 1 homolog) interacts with and is required for EAT-16 activity (Porter and Koelle, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hajdu-Cronin et al., 1999.

claims.claim: RSBP-1 interacts with and is required for EAT-16 activity.
claims.source: The RGS (regulator of G protein signaling) protein EAT-16 terminates Gq signaling by activating intrinsic Gq GTPase activity (Hajdu-Cronin et al., 1999); RSBP-1 (R7 binding protein 1 homolog) interacts with and is required for EAT-16 activity (Porter and Koelle, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Porter and Koelle, 2010.

claims.claim: Disrupting either eat-16 or rsbp-1 enabled N2 animals to behave like npr-1 mutants in response to a change in O2.
claims.source: Disrupting either eat-16 or rsbp-1 enabled N2 animals, which express npr-1 215V, to behave like npr-1 mutants in response to a change in O2 (Figure 2F–H).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F-H.

claims.claim: ASK sensory neurons respond to pheromones and food.
claims.source: The ASK sensory neurons respond to pheromones and food (Macosko et al., 2009; Wakabayashi et al., 2009), and, like the URX O2 sensors, make gap junctions with RMG (White et al., 1986; wormwiring.org; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Macosko et al., 2009 and Wakabayashi et al., 2009.

claims.claim: ASK neurons make gap junctions with RMG.
claims.source: The ASK sensory neurons respond to pheromones and food (Macosko et al., 2009; Wakabayashi et al., 2009), and, like the URX O2 sensors, make gap junctions with RMG (White et al., 1986; wormwiring.org; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 1986 and wormwiring.org, and by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ASH and ADL nociceptive neurons make gap junctions with RMG.
claims.source: The ASH and ADL nociceptive neurons also make gap junctions with RMG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A switch from 7% to 21% O2 elicited a small increase in YFP/CFP FRET in ASK neurons, indicating a rise in Ca2+.
claims.source: A switch from 7% to 21% O2 elicited a small increase in YFP/CFP FRET in ASK and ASH, indicating a rise in [Ca2+] (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: A switch from 7% to 21% O2 elicited a small increase in YFP/CFP FRET in ASH neurons, indicating a rise in Ca2+.
claims.source: A switch from 7% to 21% O2 elicited a small increase in YFP/CFP FRET in ASK and ASH, indicating a rise in [Ca2+] (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in ASK and ASH were sustained while animals were at 21% O2.
claims.source: The responses were sustained while animals were at 21% O2.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: Deleting gcy-35 abolished the O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in ASK and ASH.
claims.source: Deleting gcy-35 abolished the O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in ASK and ASH (Figure 3A,B), consistent with these responses being driven by URX, and therefore potentially via RMG.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: npr-1 animals lacking ASK neurons responded to a 7-21-7% O2 regime indistinguishably from control npr-1 animals.
claims.source: npr-1 animals lacking ASK neurons responded to a 7–21–7% O2 regime indistinguishably from control npr-1 animals (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of ASK had no effect on speed in npr-1 animals.
claims.source: Optogenetic inhibition of ASK, in an npr-1 strain expressing halorhodopsin (NpHR) specifically in ASK, had no effect on speed (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Ablating ASK neurons in npr-1 animals did not impair aggregation behavior.
claims.source: Ablating ASK neurons in npr-1 animals also did not impair aggregation behavior (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ASH and ADL ablated npr-1 animals responded to high and low O2 and to current injection into RMG like npr-1 controls.
claims.source: The ASH and ADL ablated animals responded to high and low O2 and to current injection into RMG like npr-1 controls (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Tetanus toxin in the ASH and ADL neurons did not disrupt O2 responses in npr-1 animals.
claims.source: Tetanus toxin in the ASH and ADL neurons also did not disrupt O2 responses (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Tetanus toxin disrupted synaptic release from ASH and ADL as confirmed by monitoring reversals in response to a 3 mM Cu2+ drop.
claims.source: To monitor toxin expression, we used a polycistronic construct that also expressed RFP, and we confirmed that tetanus toxin disrupted synaptic release from ASH and ADL by monitoring reversals in response to a 3 mM Cu2+ drop (Figure 3F, inset).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F, inset.

claims.claim: Disrupting ocr-2 attenuates animals' ability to navigate spatial O2 gradients and to aggregate.
claims.source: The ASH and ADL neurons express the TRPV1 homolog ocr-2, and disrupting ocr-2, or its partner subunit osm-9, attenuates animals' ability to navigate spatial O2 gradients and to aggregate (de Bono et al., 2002; Chang et al., 2006; Rogers et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to de Bono et al., 2002; Chang et al., 2006; Rogers et al., 2006.

claims.claim: ocr-2; npr-1 animals only weakly modulated their locomotory activity when switched between 7% and 21% O2.
claims.source: ocr-2; npr-1 animals only weakly modulated their locomotory activity when switched between 7% and 21% O2 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Expressing ocr-2 cDNA in ASH, ADL, or ADF neurons increased the speed of ocr-2; npr-1 animals at 21% O2.
claims.source: Expressing ocr-2 cDNA in ASH or ADL or the serotonergic ADF neurons increased the speed of ocr-2; npr-1 animals at 21% O2 and, as expected, rescued the bordering and aggregation phenotype (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) (de Bono et al., 2002; Chang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The ability of ocr-2 expression in ASH or ADL neurons to rescue the speed response and aggregation behavior of ocr-2; npr-1 animals was retained when neurotransmission from these neurons was blocked using tetanus toxin.
claims.source: The ability of ocr-2 expression in ASH or ADL neurons to rescue the speed response and aggregation behavior of ocr-2; npr-1 animals was retained when neurotransmission from these neurons was blocked using tetanus toxin (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: A 10 mM Cu2+ stimulus resulted in a large, sharp rise in ASH Ca2+.
claims.source: As expected, a 10 mM Cu2+ stimulus resulted in a large, sharp rise in ASH Ca2+ that was easily detectable using YC3.60 (Hilliard et al., 2004) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and supported by a citation to Hilliard et al., 2004.

claims.claim: A 10 mM Cu2+ stimulus failed to evoke any Ca2+ responses in the RMG cell body.
claims.source: By contrast, this stimulus failed to evoke any Ca2+ responses in the RMG cell body that could be measured with YC2.60 (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The steady state Ca2+ levels in the URX or RMG cell bodies were not significantly affected by the ocr-2 mutation.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the steady state Ca2+ levels in the URX or RMG cell bodies were not significantly affected by the ocr-2 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: ChR2-activation of RMG in ocr-2; npr-1 animals stimulated rapid movement and inhibited reversals, both at 21% and 7% O2.
claims.source: Consistent with this, ChR2-activation of RMG in ocr-2; npr-1 animals stimulated rapid movement, and inhibited reversals, both at 21% and 7% O2 (Figure 4I,J and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I and 4J.

claims.claim: Cultivating animals in 7% O2 reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in both URX and AUA.
claims.source: Cultivating animals in 7% O2, or deleting gcy-35, reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in both URX and AUA (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Deleting gcy-35 reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in both URX and AUA.
claims.source: Cultivating animals in 7% O2, or deleting gcy-35, reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in both URX and AUA (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Knocking out ocr-2 did not alter pflp-11::gfp expression in URX or AUA.
claims.source: By contrast, knocking out ocr-2 did not, suggesting that TRPV signaling did not alter URX or AUA peptide expression (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The genotype at the npr-1 locus did not affect pflp-11::gfp expression in URX.
claims.source: The genotype at the npr-1 locus did not affect pflp-11::gfp expression in URX, but expression in the AUA neurons was reduced in animals encoding the npr-1 215V allele compared to npr-1 null mutants (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: pflp-11::gfp expression in AUA neurons was reduced in animals encoding the npr-1 215V allele compared to npr-1 null mutants.
claims.source: The genotype at the npr-1 locus did not affect pflp-11::gfp expression in URX, but expression in the AUA neurons was reduced in animals encoding the npr-1 215V allele compared to npr-1 null mutants (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: pflp-11::gfp expression in SAB was not affected by O2 experience or the genotypes tested.
claims.source: pflp-11::gfp expression in SAB, a neuron not known to be modulated by O2, was not affected either by O2 experience or the genotypes tested, providing an internal control.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: Expression of EGL-2(GF) strongly reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in URX.
claims.source: EGL-2(GF) expression strongly reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in URX (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Tetanus toxin expression strongly reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in URX.
claims.source: Tetanus toxin expression strongly reduced pflp-11::gfp expression in URX, and the effect was stronger when toxin expression was higher (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: pflp-5::gfp expression in RMG was higher in npr-1 animals grown at 21% O2 than in npr-1 animals grown at 7% O2 or gcy-35; npr-1 mutants grown at 21% O2.
claims.source: pflp-5::gfp expression in RMG was higher in npr-1 animals grown at 21% O2 than in npr-1 animals grown at 7% O2 or gcy-35; npr-1 mutants grown at 21% O2 (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Expression of pflp-5::GFP in the M4 pharyngeal neuron was not altered by O2 experience or by disrupting gcy-35.
claims.source: In contrast, expression of pflp-5::GFP in the M4 pharyngeal neuron, which is not known to respond to O2, was not altered by O2 experience or by disrupting gcy-35.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: Animals expressing tetanus toxin in RMG showed significantly less pflp-5 expression in RMG than non-expressing siblings.
claims.source: Animals expressing tetanus toxin in RMG showed significantly less pflp-5 expression in RMG than non-expressing siblings (Figure 5E), consistent with neurosecretion feeding back to stimulate pflp-5 transcription.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Expression of pflp-5::gfp in RMG was reduced in N2 animals compared to npr-1 mutants, both at 21% and 7% O2.
claims.source: Expression of pflp-5::gfp in RMG was reduced in N2 animals compared to npr-1 mutants, both at 21% and 7% O2.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claims.claim: ocr-2; npr-1 animals kept at 21% O2 showed reduced pflp-5::gfp expression compared to npr-1 worms kept at the same O2 levels.
claims.source: Interestingly, ocr-2; npr-1 animals kept at 21% O2 also showed reduced pflp-5::gfp expression compared to npr-1 worms kept at the same O2 levels (Figure 5D), suggesting that disrupting ocr-2 reduced RMG neurosecretion in npr-1 animals.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Expression of the long pflp-21::GFP transgene in RMG and RMH was highest in npr-1 animals cultivated at 21% O2.
claims.source: Expression of the long pflp-21::GFP transgene in RMG and RMH was highest in npr-1 animals cultivated at 21% O2, and reduced in gcy-35; npr-1 and ocr-2; npr-1 animals grown at 21% O2, as well as npr-1 animals kept overnight at 7% O2 (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: pflp-21::GFP transgene expression in RMG and RMH was reduced in N2 animals compared to npr-1 mutants, both at 21% and 7% O2.

results.result: Exposure to 21% O2 induces sustained locomotory arousal in C. elegans npr-1 mutants, characterized by increased speed and persistent forward movement through inhibition of spontaneous reversals. This behavioral response requires functional GCY-35 in URX neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 provide direct experimental evidence showing that npr-1 animals increase speed and suppress reversals at 21% O2 (Figures 1A-C), that gcy-35 mutations disrupt this response, and that selective URX rescue restores the phenotype. The data demonstrate both necessity (gcy-35 requirement) and sufficiency (URX-specific rescue) of the O2-sensing pathway.

results.result: URX O2-sensing neurons drive arousal at 21% O2 by tonically activating RMG interneurons through gap junctions and reciprocal synaptic connections. URX ablation eliminates O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in RMG, and RMG ablation reduces URX Ca2+ responses, indicating bidirectional communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 establish that RMG responds to O2 with sustained Ca2+ increases and that URX ablation eliminates these responses (Figure 1D). Claims C79-C81 demonstrate reciprocal regulation, with RMG ablation reducing URX responses and unc-64 syntaxin mutants showing reduced Ca2+ in both neurons. The anatomical connectivity (C67) and functional data converge to support the URX→RMG circuit model.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of RMG using channelrhodopsin-2 is sufficient to induce rapid forward movement and suppress reversals in npr-1 animals, even when URX, AQR, and PQR neurons are ablated. RMG activation effects summate with endogenous O2 circuit input.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 demonstrate sufficiency using ChR2 activation (Figures 1E-F), while C77-C78 show this effect persists after O2-sensor ablation (Figures 1G-I), ruling out feedback through URX. Claim C76 shows graded responses with O2 levels, indicating summation. The optogenetic experiments provide strong causal evidence that RMG activation alone can switch behavioral state.

results.result: ASK, ASH, and ADL sensory neurons connected to RMG by gap junctions are not required for O2-evoked arousal. Ablation or optogenetic inhibition of ASK, or ablation/tetanus toxin expression in ASH and ADL, does not disrupt behavioral responses to 21% O2.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent manipulations (ablation C105, C108; optogenetics C106; tetanus toxin C109-C110) consistently show that these neurons are dispensable for O2 responses (Figures 3C-F). The tetanus toxin control (C110) confirms functional blockade. This contradicts prior hub-and-spoke models suggesting these neurons are necessary outputs, but the experimental evidence is robust.

results.result: OCR-2 TRPV channel activity in ASH, ADL, or ADF neurons is required for full O2-evoked arousal, but this requirement is independent of neurotransmission from these neurons. Disrupting ocr-2 attenuates locomotory responses to 21% O2, which can be rescued by cell-specific ocr-2 expression or by direct RMG stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 shows ocr-2 mutants have reduced O2 responses (Figure 4A). Claims C113-C114 demonstrate rescue by cell-specific ocr-2 expression that persists with tetanus toxin blockade (Figures 4B-C), indicating a non-synaptic mechanism. Claim C119 shows ChR2 activation of RMG bypasses the ocr-2 requirement (Figures 4I-J), placing OCR-2 function upstream of RMG output. The tetanus toxin control is critical for ruling out synaptic mechanisms.

results.result: NPR-1 215V receptor signaling in RMG, activated by FLP-21 peptide, selectively suppresses sustained O2-evoked locomotory changes without affecting transient avoidance responses. NPR-1 215V acts primarily downstream of Ca2+ influx to inhibit RMG output.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 show cell-specific NPR-1 215V expression in RMG blocks sustained but not transient O2 responses (Figure 2, Figure 2—supplement 1). Claims C88-C89 demonstrate flp-21 deletion enhances responses in NPR-1-expressing animals (Figures 2A-C). Critically, claims C92-C93 show that despite similar or lower Ca2+ levels, N2 animals respond much less to RMG ChR2 activation than npr-1 mutants (Figures 2D-E), supporting a post-Ca2+ mechanism. The logic is sound and experiments are well-controlled.

results.result: NPR-1 inhibits neurotransmission by coupling to Go/i signaling, which can be opposed by disrupting the Gq-inhibiting RGS protein EAT-16 or its binding partner RSBP-1. Mutations in eat-16 or rsbp-1 enable N2 animals to respond to O2 like npr-1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 cites in vitro evidence for NPR-1 coupling to Go/i. Claims C95-C96 establish that EAT-16/RSBP-1 inhibit Gq signaling. Claim C97 provides genetic evidence that disrupting these Gq inhibitors phenocopies npr-1 loss (Figures 2F-H). The model is internally consistent: if NPR-1 activates Go to inhibit release, then reducing Gq inhibition should restore release. The genetic epistasis supports the proposed mechanism.

results.result: RMG signals high O2 primarily through peptidergic secretion. Blocking neurosecretion from RMG with tetanus toxin or RNAi knockdown of the neuropeptide-processing enzyme egl-21 eliminates O2-evoked behavioral responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142 show that tetanus toxin or egl-21 RNAi in RMG abolishes O2 responses (Figures 6A-D). These manipulations specifically target neuropeptide release (tetanus toxin blocks all secretion; egl-21 is required for neuropeptide maturation). The loss-of-function phenotypes are complete, indicating peptidergic signaling is the major output mechanism. The experiments directly test the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Neuropeptide gene transcription is positively coupled to neurosecretory activity, providing a readout of circuit state. Expression of neuropeptide reporters (pflp-11, pflp-5, pflp-21) is regulated by O2 levels, neural activity, and neurosecretion, and can be disrupted by inhibiting neurons or blocking secretion with tetanus toxin.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121, C128 show O2-dependent regulation of neuropeptide reporters (Figure 5A, D). Claims C126-C127, C130 demonstrate that inhibiting neurons (EGL-2(GF)) or blocking secretion (tetanus toxin) reduces reporter expression (Figures 5B-C, E). Claim C178-C179 establish the feedback acts downstream of Ca2+. The multiple independent manipulations (O2, genetic inhibition, toxin) converging on the same conclusion provide strong support. This is a novel methodological contribution.

results.result: In freely moving animals, URX and RMG neurons encode O2 concentration rather than behavior, showing sustained Ca2+ increases at 21% O2 that do not change during reversals or speed changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C150 show RMG exhibits tonic O2-dependent Ca2+ that doesn't correlate with behavioral transitions (Figure 8B). Claim C160 confirms this pattern (Figure 9G). The freely-moving imaging experiments are technically challenging but provide critical evidence that these neurons encode sensory state rather than motor output. The distinction between sensory encoding and motor execution is well-supported.

results.result: AVB and AIY interneurons integrate O2 information with behavioral execution. Their Ca2+ levels show rapid fluctuations correlated with behavioral transitions, but average Ca2+ is higher at 21% O2 than 7% O2, indicating tonic O2 modulation superimposed on phasic behavioral signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C152 establish that AVB and AIY show rapid Ca2+ changes coinciding with behavioral transitions (Figures 8C-G). Claims C153-C154, C158-C159 demonstrate statistically significant O2-dependent differences in average Ca2+ during forward locomotion (Figures 9B-C). This dual encoding—both O2 level and behavior—is a key finding distinguishing these neurons from URX/RMG. The statistical analysis of event-triggered averages is appropriate.

results.result: AIA, AIB, and AVA interneurons participate in executing behavioral state but are not tonically modulated by O2. AIA inhibits reversals at 21% O2 through inhibitory control of AVA, as shown by optogenetic manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C157 show these neurons lack O2-dependent Ca2+ modulation (Figures 9D-F). Claims C161-C162 demonstrate that optogenetic inhibition of AIA increases reversals at 21% O2 (Figure 10B). Claims C163-C164 show AIA inhibition/disinhibition causes corresponding AVA Ca2+ changes (Figures 10E-F). The optogenetic experiments establish causal relationships. These neurons execute behavior but don't encode O2 state, consistent with a hierarchical circuit organization.

results.result: AIY interneurons promote rapid forward movement and suppress reversals at 21% O2. Optogenetic activation of AIY increases speed and decreases reversals, while ttx-3 mutants lacking AIY show reduced speed responses to O2 but normal reversal suppression.
results.evaluation: Claim C165 shows AIY activation phenocopies high O2 effects. Claims C166-C167 show ttx-3 mutants have partial defects (Figures 10G-H). Claim C168 shows AIA ablation in ttx-3 background increases reversals (Figures 10I-J), suggesting redundancy. The optogenetic gain-of-function and genetic loss-of-function experiments converge on AIY's role in speed control. The partial phenotype in ttx-3 suggests other neurons contribute, which is acknowledged.

results.result: 21% O2 alters expression of genes encoding neuropeptides, metabolic enzymes, and other non-neural proteins in a GCY-35-dependent manner. RNA-seq identified 72 genes whose O2-dependent expression requires functional O2 sensors, including genes involved in metabolism, oxidation-reduction, and proteolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 provide quantitative RNA-seq data showing overlap between O2-regulated and GCY-35-dependent genes (Supplementary file 4). Claims C60-C62 identify functional categories of regulated genes. The experimental design comparing npr-1 at different O2 levels and gcy-35; npr-1 mutants appropriately controls for O2-independent effects. The q-value cutoff of 0.05 is standard. This demonstrates O2 sensing has broad transcriptional effects beyond the nervous system.

results.result: ASK and ASH neurons show small, sustained Ca2+ increases in response to 7-21% O2 shifts that are abolished in gcy-35 mutants, suggesting these responses are driven by URX input, potentially via RMG.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 document O2-evoked Ca2+ responses in ASK and ASH (Figures 3A-B). Claim C104 shows gcy-35 dependence. However, the responses are described as "small" and the authors note they may be local to gap junctions rather than soma-wide. The functional significance is unclear given that ablating these neurons doesn't affect O2 responses (C105-C110). The data support the claim but its biological importance is uncertain.

results.result: Strong activation of ASH with Cu2+ does not evoke detectable Ca2+ responses in the RMG cell body, and ocr-2 mutations do not significantly affect steady-state Ca2+ levels in URX or RMG cell bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 show Cu2+ stimulation produces large ASH Ca2+ responses but no RMG responses (Figures 4E-F). Claim C118 shows ocr-2 doesn't affect somatic Ca2+ in URX/RMG. These negative results are important for ruling out certain mechanisms (e.g., ASH→RMG Ca2+ flow through gap junctions) and support the authors' model that OCR-2 effects are local to gap junctions. The negative controls are well-executed.

results.result: The pflp-21 promoter drives lower YC2.60 expression in RMG in N2 animals compared to npr-1 mutants, and lower sensor expression correlates with lower YFP/CFP ratios at 21% O2.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 document technical issues with Ca2+ sensor expression that complicate interpretation of N2 vs npr-1 comparisons (Figure 2—supplement 2). This is an important methodological caveat. The authors appropriately acknowledge this confound and use alternative approaches (optogenetics, neuropeptide reporters) to support their conclusions about NPR-1 function. The transparency about technical limitations strengthens confidence in the overall conclusions.

results.result: The genotype at the npr-1 locus affects pflp-11::gfp expression in AUA but not URX neurons, while ocr-2 mutations do not alter expression in either neuron. Expression in the control neuron SAB is unaffected by O2 or genotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 describe cell-specific effects of genetic manipulations on neuropeptide reporter expression (Figure 5A). The SAB control (C125) is important for validating the specificity of O2/genetic effects. These observations support the model that NPR-1 and OCR-2 have distinct, cell-specific effects on circuit function. The data are clearly presented.

results.result: Expression of pflp-5::GFP in the M4 pharyngeal neuron is not regulated by O2 or gcy-35, while expression in RMG is reduced in N2 animals and ocr-2; npr-1 mutants compared to npr-1 animals at 21% O2.
results.evaluation: Claims C129, C131-C134 document cell-specific and genotype-specific regulation of pflp-5 expression (Figure 5D). The M4 control (C129) validates specificity. The ocr-2 effect on RMG expression (C132) provides additional evidence that OCR-2 activity influences RMG neurosecretion. These observations support the broader model of circuit regulation.

results.result: OCR-2 TRPV channel activity is required for pflp-21 expression in ASH and ADL neurons, as shown by reduced expression in ocr-2 mutants and with tetanus toxin. O2 levels do not significantly modulate pflp-21 expression in these neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C137 show OCR-2-dependent but O2-independent regulation of pflp-21 in ASH/ADL (Figures 5G-H). This is consistent with the model that OCR-2 provides tonic/chronic activity in these neurons rather than responding to O2 changes. The tetanus toxin control (C136) confirms the expression-secretion coupling. These data support the mechanistic model.

results.result: Expression of ppdf-1::gfp in PVP and AVB is upregulated at 21% O2, pflp-17::gfp in BAG is upregulated at 7% O2, and pflp-3::gfp in IL1 is not regulated by O2 or npr-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 document O2 regulation of additional neuropeptide reporters in various neurons (Figures 5I-K). The IL1 control (C140) demonstrates specificity. These observations extend the finding that O2 modulates neuropeptide expression across multiple neurons, supporting the model of widespread circuit state changes. The data are descriptive but contribute to the overall picture.

results.result: In immobilized animals, Ca2+ levels in AVA/AVB and A/B motoneurons are anti-correlated and show stochastic switches lasting over a minute. O2 upsteps activate VA neurons and modulate average AVB and AIY activity despite frequent switches.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C148 describe Ca2+ dynamics in immobilized animals (Figures 7A-D). The anti-correlation (C144-C145) replicates prior work (Kawano 2011). The stochastic switching (C146) is noted as "fictive behavior" that differs from freely moving animals. Claims C147-C148 show O2 can modulate this activity. These observations validate the imaging approach but the immobilization artifact limits interpretation. The authors appropriately focus on freely moving data for main conclusions.

results.result: Stimulating RMG does not elicit transient avoidance responses evoked by O2 increases, suggesting distinct circuits coordinate transient and persistent behavioral changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C170 note that RMG stimulation produces sustained but not transient responses (Discussion). This is consistent with C84 showing NPR-1 215V expression in RMG blocks sustained but not transient responses. The inference that separate circuits mediate these responses is reasonable but not directly tested. Additional experiments (e.g., identifying neurons mediating transient responses) would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: C. elegans uses 21% O2 as an indicator of hazardous surface exposure and responds with sustained arousal lasting at least 2 hours. O2 concentration is 21% at the surface but lower in buried spaces due to respiration.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the biological context and prior knowledge (C35-C40 cite previous work; C1, C36, C37 state general principles). Claim C52 summarizes the interpretation that C. elegans perceives 21% O2 as a threat. The supporting citations are appropriate and the ecological logic is sound. This provides important context but is primarily background rather than new findings.

results.result: Mammals and invertebrates adopt different global states in response to various stimuli (mates, predators, nutritional state) involving coordinated changes in physiology, neurochemistry, arousal, and sensory processing. Prior work in mice and Drosophila has identified neurons that can induce specific behavioral states.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C34 provide extensive background on global states in mammals and invertebrates, citing numerous prior studies. These establish the conceptual framework and prior art. The citations appear appropriate (LeDoux 2012, Lin 2011, Tye 2011, etc.). This is standard introduction material that contextualizes the current work but doesn't present new findings.

results.result: Prior work established that URX, AQR, and PQR O2-sensing neurons drive avoidance and escape from 21% O2 through a GCY-35/GCY-36 soluble guanylate cyclase, cGMP channels, and L-type Ca2+ channels. These neurons show tonic responses and regulate multiple behaviors and physiological processes. The NPR-1 215V mutation in N2 prevents study of these responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C56 comprehensively review prior work on C. elegans O2 sensing, citing multiple papers from the field (Gray 2004, Cheung 2004-2005, Zimmer 2009, Busch 2012, etc.). The citations appear accurate and comprehensive. Claim C53 explains why npr-1 mutants are used in this study. This is essential background that establishes what was known before the current work.

results.result: Neuropeptides are used across phylogeny to create, maintain, or amplify neuronal network states.
results.evaluation: Claim C172 cites Marder et al. 2014 to support a general principle about neuropeptide function. This provides context for the finding that RMG uses peptidergic signaling. The citation is appropriate and the statement is well-established in the field.

results.result: The authors speculate that NPR-1's main inhibitory role is downstream of Ca2+ influx and may involve altering the balance between Go and Gq signaling in favor of Go.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C181 are explicitly speculative ("led us to speculate," "may inhibit"). While the speculation is informed by the data (post-Ca2+ effects, genetic interactions with eat-16/rsbp-1), direct evidence for the proposed Go/Gq mechanism is lacking. The in vitro data (C94) shows NPR-1 can couple to Go/i, but whether this occurs in vivo and how it mechanistically inhibits release is not demonstrated. This is a reasonable hypothesis requiring further testing.
